speaker: Doctor
text: Welcome to my office. I understand you have knee pain after increasing your physical activity. To help me narrow this down, please describe exactly where the pain is located and what movements make it worse?

speaker: Patient
text: 23-year-old female. The patient presents with knee pain that started yesterday and has been steadily worsening. She cites recent participation in volleyball involving repetitive pivoting and twisting movements as a possible cause. She was advised at her last physical exam that weight loss could be beneficial for her health.

speaker: Doctor
text: Thank you for that history. To clarify the location and severity: is the pain on the inner (medial), outer (lateral), front, or back of the knee, and does it feel like a sharp pop or just soreness? Also, can you bear weight on that leg right now, and is there visible swelling or bruising?

speaker: Patient
text: My main symptom is Knee pain, specifically over the medial aspect of the tibia just inferior to the patella. I also have Recent weight loss attempt, Increased physical activity.

speaker: Doctor
text: That specific location—over the medial tibial tuberosity—is highly characteristic of Osgood-Schlatter disease, though your age makes it less common; did you notice a tender bump or a hard nodule on the bone at that spot? speaker: Doctor
text:
DIAGNOSIS READY: Osgood-Schlatter disease (or tibial tubercle apophysitis).

The pain location over the medial tibial tuberosity, combined with your age and recent increase in pivoting sports like volleyball, is highly characteristic of this condition. The X-ray I requested will confirm the presence of apophysitis or bony traction spurs to finalize the diagnosis.
